name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANICCHEMISTRY_AR_Q01 - Electronegativity of sp hybridised carbon

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): A carbon atom having an \(sp\) hybrid orbital is more electronegative than a carbon atom possessing \(sp^2\) or \(sp^3\) hybridised orbitals.

Reason (R): An \(sp\) hybrid orbital has \(50\%\) \(s\)-character, which holds the electrons closer to the nucleus than \(sp^2\) (\(33.3\%\) \(s\)-character) or \(sp^3\) (\(25\%\) \(s\)-character) hybrid orbitals.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electronegativity of a hybridised carbon atom depends on the percentage of \(s\)-character in its hybrid orbitals. Because \(s\)-orbitals are spherical and penetrate closer to the nucleus than \(p\)-orbitals, electrons in orbitals with higher \(s\)-character experience a stronger nuclear attraction.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In organic compounds, \(sp\) hybridised carbon (as in ethyne) exhibits higher electronegativity than \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon (as in ethene) and \(sp^3\) hybridised carbon (as in methane). Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
An \(sp\) hybrid orbital consists of one \(s\) and one \(p\) orbital, giving \(50\%\) \(s\)-character, compared to \(33.3\%\) in \(sp^2\) and \(25\%\) in \(sp^3\). Greater \(s\)-character brings the orbital closer to the nucleus and increases the effective attraction on bonding electrons. Thus, the reason is correct and directly explains why \(sp\) carbon is more electronegative.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect but (R) is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANICCHEMISTRY_AR_Q02 - Restricted rotation about carbon-carbon double bond

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Rotation of one \(\mathrm{CH}_2\) fragment with respect to the other about the \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond in ethene is restricted.

Reason (R): A \(\pi\)-bond is formed by the head-on (axial) overlap of two \(p\)-orbitals along the internuclear axis.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A \(\pi\)-bond is formed by the sideways (lateral) overlap of two parallel unhybridised \(p\)-orbitals located perpendicular to the plane of the molecule.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In \(\mathrm{H_2C=CH_2}\), all atoms lie in the same plane and the two \(p\)-orbitals are mutually parallel. Rotating one \(\mathrm{CH}_2\) group relative to the other disrupts this parallel alignment and breaks the sideways overlap of the \(p\)-orbitals, which makes rotation about the \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond restricted. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis forms a \(\sigma\)-bond, not a \(\pi\)-bond. A \(\pi\)-bond requires parallel orientation and sideways overlap of adjacent \(p\)-orbitals. Thus, the reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is correct, but the reason is incorrect.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect but (R) is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANICCHEMISTRY_AR_Q03 - Hyperconjugation and stability of carbocations

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The tert-butyl carbocation, \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{C}^+\), is more stable than the ethyl carbocation, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2^+\).

Reason (R): \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{C}^+\) has nine \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds on alkyl groups directly attached to the positively charged carbon for hyperconjugation, whereas \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2^+\) has only three such \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hyperconjugation is a permanent stabilising interaction involving the delocalisation of \(\sigma\)-electrons from \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds of an alkyl group directly attached to a positively charged carbon atom with an empty \(p\)-orbital. Greater the number of such \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds, greater is the dispersal of positive charge and higher is the stability of the carbocation.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Among alkyl carbocations, stability follows the order \(\mathrm{CH}_3^+ < \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2^+ < (\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{CH}^+ < (\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{C}^+\). Therefore, the tert-butyl carbocation is more stable than the ethyl carbocation, so the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
In \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{C}^+\), there are three methyl groups directly bonded to the positively charged \(sp^2\) carbon, providing \(3 \times 3 = 9\) \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds for hyperconjugation. In \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2^+\), there is only one methyl group, providing \(3\) \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds. Thus, the reason is correct and explains the greater stability of \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{C}^+\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect but (R) is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANICCHEMISTRY_AR_Q04 - Inductive effect and acidity of chloroacetic acids

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Trichloroacetic acid (\(\mathrm{Cl}_3\mathrm{CCOOH}\)) is a stronger acid than dichloroacetic acid (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2\mathrm{CHCOOH}\)).

Reason (R): Alkyl groups such as methyl (\(-\mathrm{CH}_3\)) and ethyl (\(-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\)) act as electron-donating groups relative to hydrogen through the inductive effect.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the inductive effect, substituents either withdraw or donate electron density relative to hydrogen. Electron-withdrawing groups (such as halogens) stabilise the carboxylate anion formed after proton loss and increase the acidity of carboxylic acids, whereas electron-donating alkyl groups decrease acidity.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
\(\mathrm{Cl}_3\mathrm{CCOOH}\) has three electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms, while \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\mathrm{CHCOOH}\) has two. Greater electron withdrawal in \(\mathrm{Cl}_3\mathrm{CCOOH}\) disperses the negative charge on the conjugate base more effectively, making \(\mathrm{Cl}_3\mathrm{CCOOH}\) a stronger acid. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Alkyl groups like \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\) and \(-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\) are indeed classified as electron-donating groups relative to hydrogen under the inductive effect. Thus, the reason is also correct, but it describes the behaviour of alkyl groups rather than the electron-withdrawing effect of chlorine atoms responsible for the acidity order of chloroacetic acids.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect but (R) is correct.

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The electromeric effect is a permanent electron displacement effect observed in molecules containing multiple bonds even in the absence of an attacking reagent.

Reason (R): When inductive and electromeric effects operate in opposite directions, the electromeric effect predominates.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electron displacement effects are classified into permanent effects (inductive, resonance, and hyperconjugation) that operate in the ground state, and temporary effects (electromeric effect) that occur only on the demand of an attacking reagent.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
The electromeric effect involves the complete transfer of a shared pair of \(\pi\)-electrons to one of the atoms joined by a multiple bond in the presence of an attacking reagent, and the effect is annulled as soon as the attacking reagent is removed. Therefore, it is a temporary effect, not a permanent one. Thus, the assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
When both inductive and electromeric effects operate in opposite directions in a molecule with a multiple bond during a reaction, the electromeric effect predominates over the inductive effect. Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is incorrect, but the reason is correct.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANICCHEMISTRY_AR_Q06 - Resonance hybrid and bond lengths in benzene

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): All carbon-carbon bond lengths in benzene are equal (\(139\text{ pm}\)), which is intermediate between a \(\mathrm{C-C}\) single bond (\(154\text{ pm}\)) and a \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond (\(134\text{ pm}\)).

Reason (R): The actual structure of benzene is a resonance hybrid of two energetically identical canonical structures having alternating single and double bonds.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to resonance theory, when a molecule cannot be adequately represented by a single Lewis structure, its actual structure is a resonance hybrid of two or more hypothetical canonical (contributing) structures.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Experimentally, benzene does not exhibit two different \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond lengths; instead, every carbon-carbon bond has an identical length of \(139\text{ pm}\), lying between typical \(\mathrm{C-C}\) single (\(154\text{ pm}\)) and \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double (\(134\text{ pm}\)) bond lengths. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Benzene is represented equally well by two energetically identical canonical structures with alternating single and double bonds. Because both contribute equally to the resonance hybrid, all six \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bonds acquire partial double-bond character and equal length. Thus, the reason is correct and explains the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANICCHEMISTRY_AR_Q07 - IUPAC nomenclature priority of keto and hydroxyl groups

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The IUPAC name of the compound \(\mathrm{HOCH}_2(\mathrm{CH}_2)_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{COCH}_3\) is 7-hydroxyheptan-2-one and not 2-oxoheptan-7-ol.

Reason (R): In the IUPAC order of decreasing priority for functional groups, the hydroxyl (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)) group is given higher preference than the keto (\(>\mathrm{C=O}\)) group.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In polyfunctional organic compounds, one functional group is chosen as the principal functional group (indicated by a suffix) based on the IUPAC priority order, while subordinate functional groups are named as prefixes.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
The compound \(\mathrm{HOCH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{COCH}_3\) has a 7-carbon chain containing both a keto (\(>\mathrm{C=O}\)) group and a hydroxyl (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)) group. Since the keto group is preferred over the hydroxyl group, it becomes the principal functional group (suffix "-one") and numbering starts from the end closer to the keto group (giving C-2 for \(>\mathrm{C=O}\) and C-7 for \(-\mathrm{OH}\)). Hence, the name is 7-hydroxyheptan-2-one. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
According to the IUPAC order of decreasing priority (\(-\mathrm{COOH} > -\mathrm{SO}_3\mathrm{H} > -\mathrm{COOR} > -\mathrm{COCl} > -\mathrm{CONH}_2 > -\mathrm{CN} > -\mathrm{CHO} > {>\mathrm{C=O}} > -\mathrm{OH} > -\mathrm{NH}_2\)), the keto (\(>\mathrm{C=O}\)) group has higher priority than the hydroxyl (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)) group, not lower. Thus, the reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is correct, but the reason is incorrect.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In steam distillation, a steam-volatile and water-immiscible organic liquid such as aniline vaporises at a temperature below its normal boiling point.

Reason (R): During steam distillation, the liquid mixture boils when the sum of the vapour pressure of the organic liquid (\(p_1\)) and that of water (\(p_2\)) equals the atmospheric pressure (\(p\)), so \(p_1 < p\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A pure liquid boils at the temperature where its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external atmospheric pressure. In a mixture of two immiscible liquids, each component exerts its own vapour pressure independently, so the total vapour pressure is the sum of the two partial vapour pressures.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Aniline (normal boiling point \(457\text{ K}\)) is steam volatile and immiscible with water. When subjected to steam distillation, the aniline-water mixture boils close to but below \(373\text{ K}\), which is well below the normal boiling point of aniline. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
In steam distillation, boiling occurs when \(p = p_1 + p_2\), where \(p_1\) is the vapour pressure of the organic liquid, \(p_2\) is the vapour pressure of water, and \(p\) is the atmospheric pressure. Since \(p_2 > 0\), \(p_1\) must be lower than \(p\), allowing the organic liquid to vaporise at a lower temperature than its normal boiling point. Thus, the reason is correct and explains the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANICCHEMISTRY_AR_Q09 - Lassaigne test when nitrogen and sulphur are both present

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): When an organic compound containing both nitrogen and sulphur is fused with a limited (non-excess) amount of sodium metal, the sodium fusion extract gives a Prussian blue colour on boiling with iron(II) sulphate and acidifying with concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\).

Reason (R): When both nitrogen and sulphur are present in the organic compound, sodium fusion produces sodium thiocyanate (\(\mathrm{NaSCN}\)), which reacts with \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) ions to form a blood-red \([\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{SCN})]^{2+}\) complex.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Lassaigne's test, covalent elements in an organic compound are converted into ionic sodium salts by fusion with sodium metal. When both nitrogen and sulphur are present (without excess sodium), sodium thiocyanate is formed: \(\mathrm{Na} + \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{N} + \mathrm{S} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaSCN}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Because sodium thiocyanate is formed instead of free sodium cyanide (\(\mathrm{NaCN}\)), there are no free cyanide ions in the extract to form ferriferrocyanide (Prussian blue). Instead, a blood-red colour is obtained and no Prussian blue colour appears (unless fusion is carried out with excess sodium, which decomposes \(\mathrm{NaSCN}\) into \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) and \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}\)). Thus, the assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The \(\mathrm{SCN}^-\) ion from \(\mathrm{NaSCN}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) ions to give \([\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{SCN})]^{2+}\), which has a characteristic blood-red colour. Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is incorrect, but the reason is correct.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect but (R) is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANICCHEMISTRY_AR_Q10 - Limitations and principle of Kjeldahl method

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Kjeldahl's method is not applicable for estimating nitrogen in compounds such as pyridine and nitrobenzene.

Reason (R): In Kjeldahl's method, the nitrogen-containing compound is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid to convert nitrogen into ammonium sulphate, and the ammonia subsequently liberated with \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is absorbed in a known excess of standard \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) solution.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kjeldahl's method relies on quantitative conversion of organic nitrogen into ammonium sulphate by digestion with concentrated sulphuric acid, followed by liberation and titration of ammonia.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Kjeldahl's method cannot be used for compounds containing nitrogen in nitro (\(-\mathrm{NO}_2\)) and azo (\(-\mathrm{N=N}-\)) groups or nitrogen present in a ring (such as pyridine) because the nitrogen in these compounds does not change into ammonium sulphate under the digestion conditions. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The reason accurately describes the experimental procedure of Kjeldahl's method (digestion with conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), heating with \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), and back-titration of standard \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)). Thus, the reason is correct, but it merely states the general method and does not explain why pyridine and nitrobenzene fail to convert to ammonium sulphate.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANICCHEMISTRY_AR_Q11 - Boiling sodium extract with nitric acid before halogen test

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In Lassaigne's test for halogens, if nitrogen or sulphur is also present in the organic compound, the sodium fusion extract is first boiled with concentrated nitric acid before adding silver nitrate.

Reason (R): Boiling with concentrated nitric acid decomposes sodium cyanide and sodium sulphide formed during sodium fusion, preventing them from interfering with the silver nitrate test for halogens.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Halogens in a sodium fusion extract are detected as halide ions (\(\mathrm{X}^-\)) by acidification with \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) and addition of \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\), which precipitates \(\mathrm{AgX}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
When nitrogen or sulphur is also present in the organic compound, the sodium fusion extract contains \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) or \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}\). Therefore, the extract must first be boiled with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) before adding \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\). Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
If \(\mathrm{CN}^-\) or \(\mathrm{S}^{2-}\) ions remain in the extract, they react with \(\mathrm{Ag}^+\) from \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\) to form precipitates of \(\mathrm{AgCN}\) (white) or \(\mathrm{Ag}_2\mathrm{S}\) (black), interfering with the identification of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\), \(\mathrm{AgBr}\), and \(\mathrm{AgI}\). Boiling with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) decomposes \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) and \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}\) (expelling \(\mathrm{HCN}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\)) so that only halide ions react with \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\). Thus, the reason is correct and explains the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect but (R) is correct.
